concept: WiredTiger history store and majority commit point cache pressure
summary: Source-anchored research for WiredTiger history store and majority commit point cache pressure. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: WT-3745 describes a historical MongoDB 3.6/lookaside feedback loop in which heavy updates caused replication lag, retained majority-read history increased cache pressure, and slowed oplog reads aggravated lag. Treat this as historical mechanism evidence, not as proof of identical behavior in modern history-store releases. (low confidence)

A firsthand MongoDB 4.4-to-5.0 migration report records history-store growth during member outages despite w:1, a one-second history window, and disabled flow control; restoring members reduced the file. This is one deployment report and does not establish a general growth rate or prove that lowering the minimum window bounds retained history. (low confidence)

For the documented PSA scenario, MongoDB describes temporarily setting the unavailable or lagging secondary to votes:0 and priority:0 so the remaining primary can advance majority commits, then using rs.reconfigForPSASet when restoring the secondary. This procedure changes voting and majority-write durability and requires topology-specific evaluation. (low confidence)

WT-6681 records a reproduced case of rapid history-store disk growth with a replica-set member down and was resolved Works as Designed. File growth alone therefore does not establish a memory leak, and the ticket's initial diagnostic hypotheses should not be presented as settled root causes. (low confidence)

Increasing minSnapshotHistoryWindowInSeconds requires retaining older modified values for a longer window and can increase disk usage. Inference: reducing that window is not a guaranteed remedy for majority-lag retention, because MongoDB separately requires durable history after the lagged commit point. (medium confidence)

In a primary-secondary-arbiter replica set, an unavailable or lagging secondary can stall the majority commit point even while w:1 writes continue. Retaining post-commit-point history adds disk writes and can increase cache pressure; the oplog may also exceed its configured limit to preserve the commit point. (high confidence)

Starting with MongoDB 5.0, enableMajorityReadConcern cannot be disabled. The older workaround of disabling majority read concern is therefore not applicable to 5.0 and later deployments. (low confidence)

WT-18765 reports dirty history-store content that eviction cannot remove during the history-store checkpoint pass, with workload-specific dirty-ratio overshoots above the configured trigger. This is evidence that a dirty trigger is not a hard instantaneous ceiling, not a universal overshoot percentage. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-26)

The replication README defines oldest_timestamp as the earliest timestamp with guaranteed retained history and states that it advances with, and cannot exceed, stable_timestamp. This links retention progress to replication's safe timestamp progress; it is not solely a matter of how recently the application requested a snapshot. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

WiredTiger stores non-obsolete older record versions in the on-disk history store while the newest committed version goes to the user table. Older versions can therefore be evicted rather than all remaining resident in cache. (high confidence)

The history store is a shared internal row-store table named WiredTigerHS.wt. Its records become reclaimable according to oldest-reader and oldest-timestamp visibility, rather than solely because wall-clock time has elapsed. (low confidence)

Netdata's MongoDB monitoring guidance correlates cache fill and dirty ratios with per-node replication lag, oplog windows and member states. This provides an operational way to investigate whether replication trouble accompanies history retention rather than diagnosing from a single cache gauge. (low confidence)

The develop-branch WT_CACHE structure distinguishes history-store in-memory bytes, dirty bytes and update bytes through bytes_hs, bytes_hs_dirty and bytes_hs_updates. Its comment warns that these cached accounting values can be outdated; they are internal fields rather than a promise of identically named serverStatus metrics. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

Moving older versions out of a user page does not guarantee an equivalent drop in cache usage: history-store writes consume cache too. WT-14336 explicitly describes dirty-content movement from the data store to the history store as a source of cache pressure. (medium confidence)

Measure history-store cache residency separately from its on-disk size. Percona's serverStatus example exposes bytes belonging to the history store table in the cache, history-store on-disk size, and read/insert counters; WT-14336 adds the motivation for separate total, dirty and update-byte accounting. (medium confidence)

Retaining history does not require keeping every historical version resident in RAM: the history store exists partly so older versions can be evicted while remaining available to older readers. History retention can nevertheless increase cache and I/O work. (high confidence)

A long-running timestamped reader can prolong the lifetime of historical versions that it still needs. History-store cleanup depends on visibility to readers and the application's oldest timestamp, so committed writes from other transactions can create retained history while that reader remains open. (high confidence)

Percona's WiredTiger Details dashboard exposes cache occupancy and byte rates read into and written from the cache. These provide operational context for history-retention investigations, but those aggregate panels do not by themselves attribute activity to the history store. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-29)

Netdata's transaction diagnostic workflow combines serverStatus transaction counters with currentOp transaction ages and WiredTiger cache measurements. It supplies a way to investigate old readers alongside cache pressure; an inactive transaction counter alone should not establish the causal diagnosis. (low confidence)
